A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom as It Relates to Investment Management and Business, Revisited基本世俗智慧（二）

What I’m going to try to do today is to extend the remarks I made two years ago at the USC Business School. You were assigned a transcript of my USC talk. There’s nothing I said then that I wouldn’t repeat today. But I want to amplify what I said then.

今天我要做的，是进一步发挥两年前我在南加州大学商学院（USC Business School）所讲的内容。你们手头有我在南加大那次演讲的讲稿。当时我说的那些话，没有哪一句是我今天不会重复的。但我想把当时说过的话再展开讲一讲。

It’s perfectly clear that if Warren Buffett had never learned anything new after graduating from the Columbia Business School, Berkshire would be a pale shadow of its present self. Warren would have gotten rich, because what he learned from Ben Graham138Ben GrahamBorn in London, Benjamin Graham (1894–1976) migrated with his family to America when he was very young. His father opened an importing business that quickly failed. Despite the challenges of poverty, Graham attended and graduated from Columbia University. He took a job as a chalker on Wall Street with Newburger, Henderson & Loeb. His intelligence and capability were soon apparent, and by age 25, he was a partner at the firm. The 1929 market crash almost wiped out Graham, but he learned valuable lessons about investing. In the 1930s, Graham published a series of books on investing that became classics. Among these impressive titles are Security Analysis and The Intelligent Investor. Graham introduced the concept of intrinsic value and the wisdom of buying stocks at a discount to that value.本杰明·格雷厄姆（Benjamin Graham，1894–1976 年）生于伦敦，很小就随家人移居美国。父亲开的进出口生意很快倒闭。尽管饱受贫困之苦，格雷厄姆仍就读并从哥伦比亚大学毕业。他在华尔街的纽伯格-亨德森-洛布公司（Newburger, Henderson & Loeb）找到一份抄黑板的工作。他的才智和能力很快显现，25 岁就成了公司合伙人。1929 年的市场崩盘几乎让格雷厄姆一无所有，但他从中学到了关于投资的宝贵教训。20 世纪 30 年代，格雷厄姆出版了一系列投资著作，都成了经典，其中包括《证券分析》（Security Analysis）和《聪明的投资者》（The Intelligent Investor）。格雷厄姆提出了内在价值的概念，以及以低于内在价值的价格买入股票的智慧。 at Columbia was enough to make anybody rich. But he wouldn’t have the kind of enterprise Berkshire Hathaway is if he hadn’t kept learning.

很显然，如果沃伦·巴菲特162Howard Buffett霍华德·巴菲特（Warren Buffett）从哥伦比亚大学商学院（Columbia Business School）毕业之后没有再学任何新东西，伯克希尔（Berkshire）只会是今日这般模样的一缕黯淡残影。沃伦本来也会发财，因为他在哥伦比亚师从本杰明·格拉汉姆（Ben Graham）学到的东西，已足以让任何人致富。但若他没有持续学习，就不会有今天伯克希尔·哈撒韦（Berkshire Hathaway）这样的企业。

How do you get worldly wisdom? What system do you use to rise into the tiny top percentage of the world in terms of having sort of an elementary, practical wisdom?

你们怎样才能获得世俗智慧？你们要用一套怎样的体系，才能跻身于世上那极少数拥有基本、实用智慧的人之列？

I’ve long believed that a certain system, which almost any intelligent person can learn, works way better than the systems that most people use. As I said at the USC Business School, what you need is a latticework of mental models in your head. And you hang your actual experience and your vicarious experience that you get from reading and so forth on this latticework of powerful models. And with that system, things gradually get to fit together in a way that enhances cognition.

长久以来，我一直相信，有那么一套体系——几乎是任何聪明人都能学会的——比大多数人所用的方法有效得多。正如我在南加州大学商学院所说，你们需要的是在头脑中构建一个由各种思维模型组成的框架。然后，把你们亲身经历的经验，以及通过阅读等途径得来的间接经验，都挂在这个由强大模型构成的框架上。有了这套体系，各种知识就会逐渐融会贯通，从而增强你们的认知能力。

“What you need is a latticework of mental models in your head. And you hang your actual experience and your vicarious experience on this latticework of powerful models. And, with that system, things gradually get to fit together in a way that enhances cognition.”你所需要的，是头脑中一组由心智模型织成的框架。你把亲身经历与间接得来的经验，都挂在这组强有力的模型之上。有了这套系统，事物就会逐渐拼成一个整体，从而提升你的认知。

Your assigned reading for today included the latest annual letters from Jack Welch139Jack WelchBorn John Francis Welch Jr. in Massachusetts, Jack Welch (1935–2020) earned a PhD in chemical engineering before joining General Electric in 1960. He worked his way up the corporate ladder, becoming chairman and CEO in 1980. During his 20 years of leadership at GE, Welch increased the value of the company from $13 billion to several hundred billion dollars.杰克·韦尔奇（Jack Welch，1935–2020 年）生于马萨诸塞州，原名小约翰·弗朗西斯·韦尔奇，1960 年加入通用电气（General Electric）之前已获得化学工程博士学位。他一路晋升，1980 年出任董事长兼首席执行官。在执掌 GE 的 20 年里，韦尔奇把公司的价值从 130 亿美元提升到数千亿美元。 and Warren Buffett relating to General Electric and Berkshire Hathaway, respectively. Jack Welch has a PhD in engineering, and Warren plainly could have gotten a PhD in any field he wanted to pursue. And both gentlemen are inveterate teachers. Worldly wisdom is quite academic when you get right down to it. Look at what General Electric has achieved—and, for that matter, what Berkshire Hathaway has achieved.

你们今天的指定阅读，包括杰克·韦尔奇139Jack WelchBorn John Francis Welch Jr. in Massachusetts, Jack Welch (1935–2020) earned a PhD in chemical engineering before joining General Electric in 1960. He worked his way up the corporate ladder, becoming chairman and CEO in 1980. During his 20 years of leadership at GE, Welch increased the value of the company from $13 billion to several hundred billion dollars.杰克·韦尔奇（Jack Welch，1935–2020 年）生于马萨诸塞州，原名小约翰·弗朗西斯·韦尔奇，1960 年加入通用电气（General Electric）之前已获得化学工程博士学位。他一路晋升，1980 年出任董事长兼首席执行官。在执掌 GE 的 20 年里，韦尔奇把公司的价值从 130 亿美元提升到数千亿美元。（Jack Welch）和沃伦·巴菲特140Warren Buffett沃伦·巴菲特分别就通用电气（General Electric）和伯克希尔·哈撒韦所写的最新年度股东信。杰克·韦尔奇拥有工程学博士学位，而沃伦若是愿意，本可以拿到任何他想研究的领域的博士学位。这两位先生都是诲人不倦的教师。说到底，世俗智慧其实相当学术化。看看通用电气取得的成就——顺便说一句，也看看伯克希尔·哈撒韦取得的成就。

Of course, Warren had a professor and mentor, Ben Graham, for whom he had a great affection. Graham was so academic that when he graduated from Columbia, three different academic departments invited him into their PhD programs and asked him to start teaching immediately as part of the PhD program: literature, Greek and Latin classics, and mathematics.

当然，沃伦有一位他深为敬爱的教授兼导师，那就是格拉汉姆（Graham）。格拉汉姆治学之气如此醇厚，以至于当他从哥伦比亚大学（Columbia）毕业时，三个不同的学术院系都邀请他进入它们的博士项目，并请他一入学就开始授课：文学系、希腊与拉丁古典学系，以及数学系。

Graham had a very academic personality. I knew him. He was a lot like Adam Smith140Adam SmithBorn in a small village in Scotland, Adam Smith was an exceptional student and entered the University of Glasgow at age 14. He later attended Oxford, returned home to Glasgow, and began an academic career in logic and moral philosophy. His seminal work, The Wealth of Nations, remains the fountainhead of contemporary economic thought. Smith’s explanation of how rational self-interest drives a free-market economy greatly influenced thinkers and economists in his own day and in the generations that followed. His work forms the basis of classical economics.亚当·斯密（Adam Smith）生于苏格兰一个小村庄，天资过人，14 岁就进入格拉斯哥大学。后来他就读牛津，回到家乡格拉斯哥，开始了逻辑学和道德哲学方向的学术生涯。他的奠基之作《国富论》（The Wealth of Nations）至今仍是当代经济思想的源头。斯密对理性自利如何驱动市场经济的解释，极大地影响了同时代及后世的思想家和经济学家。他的著作构成了古典经济学的基础。—very preoccupied, very brilliant. He even looked like an academic. And he was a good one. And Graham, without ever really trying to maximize the gaining of wealth, died rich—even though he was always generous and spent 30 years teaching at Columbia and authored or coauthored the best textbooks in his field. So I would argue that academia has a lot to teach about worldly wisdom and that the best academic values really work.

格拉汉姆的性格极具学人气。我认识他。他很像亚当·斯密140Adam SmithBorn in a small village in Scotland, Adam Smith was an exceptional student and entered the University of Glasgow at age 14. He later attended Oxford, returned home to Glasgow, and began an academic career in logic and moral philosophy. His seminal work, The Wealth of Nations, remains the fountainhead of contemporary economic thought. Smith’s explanation of how rational self-interest drives a free-market economy greatly influenced thinkers and economists in his own day and in the generations that followed. His work forms the basis of classical economics.亚当·斯密（Adam Smith）生于苏格兰一个小村庄，天资过人，14 岁就进入格拉斯哥大学。后来他就读牛津，回到家乡格拉斯哥，开始了逻辑学和道德哲学方向的学术生涯。他的奠基之作《国富论》（The Wealth of Nations）至今仍是当代经济思想的源头。斯密对理性自利如何驱动市场经济的解释，极大地影响了同时代及后世的思想家和经济学家。他的著作构成了古典经济学的基础。（Adam Smith）——极其专注，极其睿智。他连长相都像个学者。而且他是位好学者。格拉汉姆从未真正着力于最大化积累财富，去世时却家财丰厚——尽管他一向慷慨，在哥伦比亚大学教了30年书，还独自或合作撰写了他那个领域最优秀的教材。所以我认为，学术界在世俗智慧方面大有可教之处，而最优秀的学术价值确实管用。

Of course, when I urge a multidisciplinary approach—that you’ve got to have the main models from a broad array of disciplines, and you’ve got to use them all—I’m really asking you to ignore jurisdictional boundaries. And the world isn’t organized that way. It discourages the jumping of jurisdictional boundaries. Big bureaucratic businesses discourage it. And, of course, academia itself discourages it. All I can say there is that, in that respect, academia is horribly wrong and dysfunctional.

当然，当我提倡跨学科方法——你们必须掌握众多学科的主要模型，并且把它们统统用上——时，我其实是在请求你们忽略学科的法定疆界。但这个世界并非按这种方式组织的。它不鼓励跨越学科疆界。庞大的官僚式企业不鼓励这样做。当然，学术界本身也不鼓励。对此我只能说，在这一方面，学术界错得离谱，而且功能失调。

Some of the worst dysfunctions in businesses come from the fact that they balkanize reality into little individual departments, with territoriality and turf protection and so forth. So if you want to be a good thinker, you must develop a mind that can jump the jurisdictional boundaries. You don’t have to know it all. Just take in the best big ideas from all these disciplines. And it’s not that hard to do.

企业中最糟糕的某些功能失调，源于它们把现实切割成一个个各自为政的小部门，充斥着地盘意识与势力范围保护之类的心态。所以，如果你们想成为优秀的思考者，就必须培养一种能够跨越学科疆界的头脑。你们不必事事通晓，只要吸收所有这些学科中最重大的思想即可。而这并不难做到。

“如果你们想成为优秀的思考者，就必须培养一种能够跨越学科疆界的头脑。”

fig 141
—
Jump the jurisdictional boundaries
“If you want to be a good thinker, you must develop a mind that can jump the jurisdictionalxa0boundaries.”若想成为优秀的思考者，你必须训练出一颗能跨越学科边界的心智。

I might try and demonstrate that point using the card game of contract bridge.143Contract bridge桥牌 Suppose you want to be good at declarer play in contract bridge. Well, you know the contract—you know what you have to achieve. And you can count up the sure winners you have by laying down your high cards and your invincible trumps. But if you’re a trick or two short, how are you going to get the other needed tricks? Well, there are only six or so different standard methods. You’ve got long suit establishment. You’ve got finesses. You’ve got throw-in plays. You’ve got crossruffs. You’ve got squeezes. And you’ve got various ways of misleading the defense into making errors. So it’s a very limited number of models. But if you only know one or two of those models, then you’re going to be a horse’s patoot in declarer play. Furthermore, these things interact. Therefore, you have to know how the models interact. Otherwise, you can’t play the hand right.

我想用定约桥牌143Contract bridge桥牌这种纸牌游戏145Card game纸牌游戏来证明这一点。假设你们想成为定约桥牌中打庄家牌的高手。嗯，你们知道定约内容——知道必须达成什么目标。你们可以摊出大牌和牢不可破的王牌，数一数自己稳拿的赢墩。但如果还差一两个赢墩，你们要怎样拿到其余所需的赢墩？标准方法其实只有六七种：可以做长套、可以飞牌、可以投入、可以交叉将吃、可以挤牌，还可以用各种方法误导防守方出错。所以模型的数量非常有限。但如果你们只知道其中一两种，打庄家牌时就会一塌糊涂。而且，这些方法彼此相互作用。因此，你们必须懂得这些模型之间如何互动，否则就无法把整手牌打好。

Similarly, I’ve told you to think forward and backward. Well, great declarers in bridge think, “How can I take the necessary winners?” But they think it through backward, too: “What could possibly go wrong that could cause me to have too many losers?” Both methods of thinking are useful. So in the game of life, get the needed models into your head and think it through forward and backward. What works in bridge will work in life.

同样地，我曾建议你们正反两面都要思考。桥牌高手会想：“我要怎样才能拿到需要的赢墩？”但他们也会反过来想：“可能会出什么岔子，导致我输掉太多墩？”两种思维方式都有用。所以在人生这场博弈中，把所需的模型装进头脑，然后正反两面都想透。桥牌中管用的，在生活中一样管用。

That contract bridge is so out of vogue in your generation is a tragedy. China is way smarter than we are about bridge. They’re teaching bridge in grade school now. And God knows the Chinese do well enough when introduced to capitalist civilization. If we compete with a bunch of people who really know how to play bridge when our people don’t, it’ll be just one more disadvantage we don’t need.

定约桥牌在你们这一代如此不流行，是件憾事。在桥牌这件事上，中国比我们聪明得多。他们现在在小学里就教桥牌了。而且天知道，中国人一旦接触资本主义文明，表现得相当出色。如果我们的人不会打桥牌，却要和一帮真正精通桥牌的人竞争，那只会给我们平添一项本不必要的劣势。

Since your academic structure, by and large, doesn’t encourage minds jumping jurisdictional boundaries, you’re at a disadvantage because, in that one sense, even though academia’s very useful to you, you’ve been mistaught. My solution for you is one that I got at a very early age, from the nursery: the story of the Little Red Hen.144The Little Red HenThe Little Red Hen is a classic fable teaching the value of self-reliance in connection with important things. Charlie’s advice on self-learning is reminiscent of Mark Twain’s classic line, “I have never let my schooling interfere with my education.”《小红母鸡》（The Little Red Hen）是一则经典寓言，讲的是在重要事情上自力更生的价值。查理关于自学的建议，让人想起马克·吐温（Mark Twain）的名言：“我从不曾让学校教育干扰我的教育。” The punch line, of course, is: “‘Then I’ll do it myself,’ said the Little Red Hen.”

既然你们的学术结构大体上不鼓励头脑跨越学科疆界，你们就处于劣势，因为从这一点上说，尽管学术界对你们非常有用，你们却受了误导式的教育。我给你们的解决办法，是我幼年时从 nursery（托儿所的童话）里得来的：小红母鸡144The Little Red HenThe Little Red Hen is a classic fable teaching the value of self-reliance in connection with important things. Charlie’s advice on self-learning is reminiscent of Mark Twain’s classic line, “I have never let my schooling interfere with my education.”《小红母鸡》（The Little Red Hen）是一则经典寓言，讲的是在重要事情上自力更生的价值。查理关于自学的建议，让人想起马克·吐温（Mark Twain）的名言：“我从不曾让学校教育干扰我的教育。”的故事。当然，点睛之笔是：“‘那我就自己来吧，’小红母鸡说。”

So if your professors won’t give you an appropriate multidisciplinary approach—if each wants to overuse his own models and underuse the important models in other disciplines—you can correct that folly yourself. Just because he’s a horse’s patoot, you don’t have to be one too. You can reach out and grasp the model that better solves the overall problem. All you have to do is know it and develop the right mental habits. And it’s kind of fun to sit there and outthink people who are way smarter than you are because you’ve trained yourself to be more objective and multidisciplinary. Furthermore, there’s a lot of money in it—as I can testify from my own personal experience.

所以，如果你们的教授不肯给你们一套恰当的跨学科方法——如果每个人都想过度使用自己的模型，而低估其他学科的重要模型——你们可以自己纠正这种愚蠢。他是一塌糊涂，不等于你们也得一塌糊涂。你们可以伸手去抓住那个能更好地解决整体问题的模型。你们所要做的，就是懂得它，并养成正确的思维习惯。坐在那儿，用自己训练出来的更客观、更跨学科的头脑，去胜过那些比你们聪明得多的人，这本身就挺有意思。而且这里面能赚大钱——这我可以用自己的亲身经历作证。

One of my favorite business stories comes from Hershey.145HersheyRaised in rural central Pennsylvania and possessed of little formal education, Milton S. Hershey (1857–1945) became one of America’s wealthiest individuals. He started his own candy business, Lancaster Caramel Company, in 1876 and failed after only six years. Undaunted, he tried again and had great success. In 1893, he learned the art of chocolate making and started the Hershey Chocolate Company. As the company expanded into other food products, Hershey began to build the Pennsylvania town that bears his name. Hershey’s utopian ideas and principles continue to influence the company and the town.米尔顿·S·好时（Milton S. Hershey，1857–1945 年）在宾夕法尼亚州中部的乡村长大，没受过多少正规教育，后来却成了美国最富有的人之一。1876 年他创办了自己的糖果公司兰卡斯特焦糖公司（Lancaster Caramel Company），仅六年后就倒闭了。他不气馁，再次尝试并大获成功。1893 年，他学会了制作巧克力的技艺，创办了好时巧克力公司（Hershey Chocolate Company）。随着公司向其他食品扩张，好时开始兴建那座以他名字命名的宾夕法尼亚小镇。好时的乌托邦理念和原则，至今仍在影响着这家公司和这座小镇。 They get their flavor because they make their cocoa butter in old stone grinders146Stone grinders石磨 that they started with in the 1800s in Pennsylvania. And a little bit of the husk of the cocoa bean147Cocoa bean可可豆 winds up in the chocolate. Therefore, they get that odd flavor that people like in Hershey’s chocolate.

我最喜欢的商业故事之一来自好时145HersheyRaised in rural central Pennsylvania and possessed of little formal education, Milton S. Hershey (1857–1945) became one of America’s wealthiest individuals. He started his own candy business, Lancaster Caramel Company, in 1876 and failed after only six years. Undaunted, he tried again and had great success. In 1893, he learned the art of chocolate making and started the Hershey Chocolate Company. As the company expanded into other food products, Hershey began to build the Pennsylvania town that bears his name. Hershey’s utopian ideas and principles continue to influence the company and the town.米尔顿·S·好时（Milton S. Hershey，1857–1945 年）在宾夕法尼亚州中部的乡村长大，没受过多少正规教育，后来却成了美国最富有的人之一。1876 年他创办了自己的糖果公司兰卡斯特焦糖公司（Lancaster Caramel Company），仅六年后就倒闭了。他不气馁，再次尝试并大获成功。1893 年，他学会了制作巧克力的技艺，创办了好时巧克力公司（Hershey Chocolate Company）。随着公司向其他食品扩张，好时开始兴建那座以他名字命名的宾夕法尼亚小镇。好时的乌托邦理念和原则，至今仍在影响着这家公司和这座小镇。（Hershey）。他们之所以有那种风味，是因为他们用19世纪在宾夕法尼亚（Pennsylvania）起家时的老式石磨146Stone grinders石磨来研磨可可脂。于是，一点点可可豆147Cocoa bean可可豆的豆壳就混进了巧克力里。也正因如此，好时巧克力才有了人们喜欢的那种独特风味。

Hershey knew enough when they wanted to expand into Canada to know they shouldn’t change their winning flavor. Therefore, they copied their stone grinders. Well, it took them five years to duplicate their own flavor. As you can see, flavors can be quite tricky. Even today, there’s a company called International Flavors and Fragrances. It’s the only company I know that does something on which you can’t get a copyright or a patent but which nevertheless receives a permanent royalty. They manage to do that by helping companies develop flavors and aromas in their trademarked products, like shaving cream.148Shaving cream剃须膏 The slight aroma of shaving cream is very important to consumption. So all of this stuff is terribly important.

My friend, Dr. Nat Myhrvold, who’s the chief technology officer at Microsoft, is bothered by this. He’s a PhD physicist and knows a lot of math. And it disturbs him that biology could create a neural apparatus that could do automatic differential equations at fast speed, and yet, everywhere he looks, people are total klutzes at dealing with ordinary probabilities and ordinary numbers.

我的朋友纳特·迈尔沃德（Nat Myhrvold）博士是微软（Microsoft）的首席技术官，他对这一点感到困扰。他是一位物理学博士，懂很多数学。让他不安的是：生物学竟能创造出一套神经装置，可以高速自动求解微分方程，然而在他眼里，人们在处理普通概率和普通数字时却一塌糊涂。

By the way, I think Myhrvold’s wrong to be amazed by that. The so-called fitness landscape of our ancestors forced them to know how to throw spears, run around, turn corners, and what have you long before they had to think correctly like Myhrvold. So I don’t think he should be so surprised. However, the difference is so extreme that I can understand how he finds it incongruous.

顺便说一句，我认为迈尔沃德对此大惊小怪是不对的。我们祖先所谓的“适应度地形”，迫使他们在还不必像迈尔沃德那样正确思考之前很久，就得懂得投矛、奔跑、拐弯等等本事。所以我觉得他本不该如此惊讶。不过，这种反差实在太极端，我能理解他为何觉得格格不入。

At any rate, mankind invented a system to cope with the fact that we are so intrinsically lousy at manipulating numbers. It’s called the graph. Oddly enough, it came out of the Middle Ages. So it’s using some of this primitive neural stuff in your system in a way that helps you understand it. In the end, Carnation came to him sheepfacedly and said, “We’d like to put our quality control inspectors into your fish plants to make sure that your fish are perfect, and we’ll pay all the costs,” which he quickly and smirkily allowed. So he got free quality control in his fish plants, courtesy of the Carnation Company.

最后，卡纳申公司涎着脸去找他说：“我们想派我们的质检员进你的鱼品厂，确保你的鱼完美无瑕，而且所有费用由我们承担。”他马上眉开眼笑地答应了。于是，他白白得到了鱼品厂的质检服务，而这全托卡纳申公司之福。

This history shows the enormous incentive you create if you give a guy a trademark. And this incentive is very useful to the wider civilization. As you see, Carnation got so that it was protecting products that it didn’t even own. That sort of outcome is very, very desirable. So there are some very fundamental microeconomic reasons why even communist countries should protect trademarks. They don’t all do it, but there are very powerful reasons why they should. And, by and large, averaged out around the world, trademark protection has been pretty good.

这段历史表明，如果你给一个人一个商标，就会创造出巨大的激励。而这种激励对整个文明都极有用处。如你所见，卡纳申后来竟去保护它根本不拥有的产品。这类结果是极为可取的。所以，即使共产主义国家，也有某些极其基本的微观经济学理由去保护商标。它们并非都这么做，但确有强有力的理由应当如此。总体而言，全世界平均来看，商标保护一直做得相当不错。

However, if you don’t have the basic models and the basic mental methods for dealing with the models, then all you can do is to sit there twiddling your thumbs as you look at the Value Line graph. But you don’t have to twiddle your thumbs. You’ve got to learn 100 models and a few mental tricks and keep doing it all of your life. It’s not that hard. And the beauty of it is that most people won’t do it—partly because they’ve been miseducated. And I’m here trying to help you avoid some of the perils that might otherwise result from that miseducation.

然而，如果你们没有基本的模型，也没有处理这些模型的基本思维方法，那么你们所能做的，就只有看着价值线的图表干瞪眼。但你们不必干瞪眼。你们得掌握100个模型，外加几个思维窍门，并且终身持之以恒。这并不难。妙处在于，大多数人不会去做——部分原因是他们受了误导式的教育。而我在此，正是想帮你们规避那种教育可能带来的某些危险。

Okay. We’ve been through some of the general ideas in the search for worldly wisdom. And now I want to turn to something even more extreme and peculiar than the talk I’ve already given you. 在人们本应以可用形式拥有、却未能拥有的所有模型中，最重要的或许位于心理学领域。

Well, the junior professor is clearly right, and Chomsky’s hesitation is a little daft. But if the junior professor and I are right, how has a genius like Chomsky made an obvious misjudgment? The answer’s quite clear to me: Chomsky is passionately ideological. He is an extreme egalitarian leftist who happens to be a genius. And he’s so smart that he realized that if he concedes this particular Darwinian point, the implications threaten his leftist ideology. So he naturally has his conclusion affected by his ideological bias. And that gets into another lesson in worldly wisdom: If ideology can screw up the head of Chomsky, imagine what it does to people like you and me.

嗯，这位资浅教授显然是对的，而乔姆斯基160Noam Chomsky诺姆·乔姆斯基的犹豫有点傻。但如果这位资浅教授和我都是对的，像乔姆斯基这样的天才怎么会犯下如此明显的判断失误？答案在我看来相当清楚：乔姆斯基充满意识形态偏见。他是一位极端的平等主义左派，碰巧又是个天才。他太聪明了，于是意识到，如果他在这个特定的达尔文论点上让步，其含义就会威胁到他的左派意识形态。所以他很自然地被自己的意识形态偏见影响了结论。这就引出了世俗智慧的又一课：如果意识形态能把乔姆斯基的脑袋搞乱，想想它会把你我这样的人弄成什么样。

Ideology does some strange things and distorts cognition terribly. If you get a lot of heavy ideology young, and then you start expressing it, you are really locking your brain into a very unfortunate pattern. And you are going to distort your general cognition.

意识形态会干出些怪事，并严重扭曲认知。如果你年轻时就沾染了大量沉重的意识形态，然后开始表达它，你其实是把自己的大脑锁进了一个非常不幸的模式。而你也将扭曲自己整体的认知能力。

“如果你年轻时就沾染了大量沉重的意识形态，然后开始表达它，你其实是把自己的大脑锁进了一个非常不幸的模式。”

“If you get a lot of heavy ideology young, and then you start expressing it, you are really locking your brain into a very unfortunatexa0pattern.”如果你年纪轻轻就装满沉重的意识形态，继而开始宣扬它，那你其实是把自己的大脑锁进了一个极不幸的模式。

There’s a very interesting history if you take Warren Buffett as an example of worldly wisdom. Warren adored his father,162Howard Buffett霍华德·巴菲特 who was a wonderful man. But Warren’s father was a very heavy ideologue—right wing, it happened to be—who hung around with other very heavy ideologues—right wing, naturally. Warren observed this as a kid, and he decided that ideology was dangerous and that he was going to stay a long way away from it. And he has throughout his whole life. That has enormously helped the accuracy of his cognition.

如果以沃伦·巴菲特作为世俗智慧的范例，会有一段很有意思的历史。沃伦深爱他的父亲，那是一位了不起的人。但沃伦的父亲是个极其固执的意识形态分子——碰巧是右翼——他成天和其他极其固执的意识形态分子——自然也是右翼——混在一起。沃伦小时候看在眼里，便认定意识形态是危险的——并决心与之保持遥远的距离。他一辈子都是这么做的。这极大地助益了他认知的准确。

I learned the same lesson in a different way. My father hated ideology. Therefore, all I had to do was imitate my father and, thereby, stay on what I regard as the right path. People like [Bob] Dornan163Bob Dornan鲍勃·多南 on the right or [Ralph] Nader164Ralph Nader拉尔夫·纳德 on the left have obviously gone a little daft. They’re extreme examples of what ideology will do to you—particularly violently expressed ideology. Since it pounds ideas in better than it convinces out, it’s a very dangerous thing to do.

我用另一种方式学到了同样的教训。我的父亲憎恶意识形态。所以我只需模仿父亲，便能走在我认为正确的道路上。像右翼的［鲍勃·］多南163Bob Dornan鲍勃·多南（Bob Dornan）或左翼的［拉尔夫·］纳德164Ralph Nader拉尔夫·纳德（Ralph Nader）那样的人，显然都有点傻了。他们是意识形态会把人变成什么样的极端例子——尤其是那种猛烈外化的意识形态。既然它灌输观念比说服人放弃更有效，做这种事就非常危险。

Therefore, in a system of multiple models across multiple disciplines, I should add as an extra rule that you should be very wary of heavy ideology. You can have heavy ideology in favor of accuracy, diligence, and objectivity. But a heavy ideology that makes you absolutely sure that the minimum wage should be raised or that it shouldn’t, and it’s kind of a holy construct where you know you’re right, makes you a bit nuts.

因此，在多学科学、多模型的体系中，我应当补加一条额外规则：你们必须对沉重的意识形态保持高度警惕。

你们可以有偏向准确、勤勉与客观的“沉重意识形态”。但如果一种沉重的意识形态让你坚信最低工资必须上调、或必须不上调，而且它成了一种你知道自己绝对正确的神圣构造，那就会让你有点神经错乱。

This is a very complicated system. And life is one damn relatedness after another. It’s all right to think that, on balance, you suspect that civilization is better if it lowers the minimum wage or raises it. Either position is okay. But being totally sure on issues like that with a strong, violent ideology, in my opinion, turns you into a lousy thinker. So beware of ideology-based mental misfunctions.

这是一套非常复杂的体系。而人生就是一连串该死的相互关联。你们认为，总体权衡之下，文明若降低最低工资、或提高最低工资会更好，这都没问题。两种立场都行。但在这类问题上，带着强烈而暴烈的意识形态去绝对确信，依我看，会把你变成糟糕的思考者。所以要警惕基于意识形态的思维失能。

Another reason that I mentioned Pinker, the semanticist who wrote the book that I told you about earlier, is that at the end of his book, he says, roughly, “I’ve read the psychology textbooks. And they’re daft.” He says, “This whole subject is misorganized and mistaught.”

我之所以又一次提到平克——那位写了刚才告诉你们的书的语义学家——还有一个原因：在书的结尾，他大致是这么说的：“我读过那些心理学教材。它们蠢透了。”他说：“整个这门学科既组织混乱，又教得糟糕。”

Well, I have far less in the way of qualifications than Pinker. In fact, I’ve never taken a single course in psychology. However, I’ve come to exactly the same conclusion—that the psychology texts, while they are wonderful in part, are also significantly daft.

嗯，我的资历比平克差远了。事实上，我从未修过一门心理学课程。然而，我得出了完全相同的结论——心理学教科书虽然部分内容精彩，但总体上也相当蠢。

In fact, just take simple psychological denial. About three centuries before the birth of Christ, Demosthenes said, “What a man wishes, that also will170James Clerk Maxwell詹姆斯·克拉克·麦克斯韦 he believe.” Well, Demosthenes was right.

其实，单看简单的心理否认就够了。在基督诞生前约三个世纪，德摩斯梯尼（Demosthenes）说：“人有所愿，便有所信。”嗯，德摩斯梯尼是对的。

“What a man wishes, that also will170James Clerk Maxwell詹姆斯·克拉克·麦克斯韦 hexa0believe.”一个人所盼望的，他也会[去相信]。

I had a family acquaintance whose much-loved son, who was brilliant and a star football player, flew off over the ocean and never came back. Well, his mother thought he was still alive. The mind will sometimes flip so that the wish becomes the belief. It will do so at various levels. Individuals vary in how much psychological denial they get. But miscognition from denial overwhelmingly pervades the reality that you’re going to have to deal with. And yet, you won’t find an adequate treatment of simple psychological denial in psychology texts.

我有个熟人的家庭，他们深爱的儿子——既聪明，又是橄榄球明星——飞越海洋后一去不返。然而他的母亲认为他还活着。心灵有时会翻转，让愿望变成信念。而且会在不同层面上发生。不同的人，心理否认的程度各异。但因否认而导致的认知错误，压倒性地弥漫在你们必将面对的现实之中。然而，心理学教材里却找不到对简单心理否认的恰当论述。

So you can’t learn psychology the way your professors teach it. You’ve got to learn everything they teach, but you’ve got to learn a lot more that they don’t teach, because they don’t handle their own subject correctly.

所以，你们不能按教授教的方式来学心理学。你们得学他们教的一切，但还必须学更多他们没教的东西，因为他们连自己的学科都没处理好。

Just open a psychology text, turn to the index, and look up envy. Well, envy made it into one or two or three of the Ten Commandments. Moses knew all about envy. 随便翻开一本心理学教材，翻到索引，查查“嫉妒”。嗯，嫉妒进了十诫中的一至三条。摩西（Moses）对嫉妒了如指掌。古时候的犹太人放羊时，对嫉妒也一清二楚。只是心理学教授们不知道嫉妒这回事。那么厚的一本书，教一门心理学课程，却不含嫉妒？没有简单的心理否认？也没有激励导致的偏见？

“Envy made it into one or two or three of the Ten Commandments. Moses knew all about envy. It’s just that psychology professors don’t know aboutxa0envy.”妒忌进了《十诫》中的一条、两条，甚至三条。摩西对妒忌了如指掌。只是心理学教授们不懂得妒忌。

And psychological texts don’t deal adequately with combinations of factors. I told you earlier to be aware of the lollapalooza effect, when two or three or more forces are operating in the same direction. Well, the single most publicized psychology experiment ever done is the Milgram170Milgram ExperimentStanley Milgram , born in 1933 in New York, grew up during World War II, when Nazi atrocities became well-known to the world. He earned a political science degree from Queens College and went on to Harvard for a PhD in social relations. He took a faculty position at Yale, where he conducted a classic experiment that pitted the subject’s moral beliefs against the demands of authority. His experiment found that 65 percent of his subjects, ordinary residents of New Haven, were willing to give apparently harmful electric shocks to a pitifully protesting victim simply because a scientific authority commanded them to, despite the fact that the victim did nothing to deserve punishment. Milgram’s results have been used as a partial explanation for the German atrocities of World War II.斯坦利·米尔格拉姆（Stanley Milgram）1933 年生于纽约，在二战期间长大，那时纳粹的暴行已为世人所知。他从皇后学院获得政治学学位，随后赴哈佛攻读社会关系学博士。他曾在耶鲁任教，在那里进行了一项经典实验，让受试者的道德信念与权威的要求相抗衡。实验发现，他的受试者中有 65%——纽黑文的普通居民——愿意仅仅因为一个科学权威的命令，就给一个可怜兮兮地抗议的受害者施加看似有害的电击，尽管那个受害者根本没做任何该受惩罚的事。米尔格拉姆的结果被部分用来解释二战中德国人的暴行。 experiment, where they asked people to apply what they had every reason to believe was heavy electrical torture on innocent fellow human beings. And they manipulated most of these decent volunteers into doing the torture. [Stanley] Milgram performed the experiment right after Hitler had gotten a bunch of believing Lutherans, Catholics, and so forth to perform unholy acts they should have known were wrong. Milgram was trying to find out how much authority could be used to manipulate high-grade people into doing things that were clearly and grossly wrong. And he got a very dramatic effect. He managed to get high-grade people to do many awful things. But for years, it was in the psychology books as a demonstration of authority—how authority could be used to persuade people to do awful things.

而且，心理学教材也没有充分处理多种因素的组合。我早先告诉过你们要警惕“lollapalooza效应”——当两三种或更多力量朝同一方向作用时。

Of course, that’s mere first-conclusion bias. That’s not the complete and correct explanation. Authority is part of it. However, there were also quite a few other psychological principles, all operating in the same direction, that achieved that lollapalooza effect precisely because they acted in combination toward the same end. People have gradually figured that out. And if you read the recent psychology texts at a place like Stanford, you’ll see that they’ve now managed to get it about two-thirds right. However, here’s the main experiment in all of psychology, and even at Stanford, they still leave out some of the important causes of Milgram’s results.

当然，那仅仅是“第一结论偏见”。那不是完整而正确的解释。权威只是其中一部分。然而，还有不少别的心理学原理，全都朝同一方向作用，正是因为它们组合发力、奔着同一个目标，才造成了那个 lollapalooza 效应。

His experiment found that 65 percent of his subjects, ordinary residents of New Haven, were willing to give apparently harmful electric shocks to a pitifully protesting victim simply because a scientific authority commanded them to, despite the fact that the victim did nothing to deserve punishment. Milgram’s results have been used as a partial explanation for the German atrocities of World War II.斯坦利·米尔格拉姆（Stanley Milgram）1933 年生于纽约，在二战期间长大，那时纳粹的暴行已为世人所知。他从皇后学院获得政治学学位，随后赴哈佛攻读社会关系学博士。他曾在耶鲁任教，在那里进行了一项经典实验，让受试者的道德信念与权威的要求相抗衡。实验发现，他的受试者中有 65%——纽黑文的普通居民——愿意仅仅因为一个科学权威的命令，就给一个可怜兮兮地抗议的受害者施加看似有害的电击，尽管那个受害者根本没做任何该受惩罚的事。米尔格拉姆的结果被部分用来解释二战中德国人的暴行。实验结果的一些重要成因。

How can smart people be so wrong? Well, the answer is that they don’t do what I’m telling you to do—which is to take all the main models from psychology and use them as a checklist in reviewing outcomes in complex systems.

聪明人怎么会错得这么离谱？答案在于，他们没做我让你们做的事——也就是把心理学中所有的主要模型都拿来，当作核查清单，用来审视复杂系统中的结果。

No pilot takes off without going through his checklist: A, B, C, D… And no bridge player who needs two extra tricks plays a hand without going down his checklist and figuring out how to do it. But these psychology professors think they’re so smart that they don’t need a checklist. But they aren’t that smart. Almost nobody is. Or maybe nobody is. If they used a checklist, they’d realize the Milgram experiment harnesses six psychological principles at least—not three. All they’d have to do is to go down the checklist to see the ones that they missed. Similarly, without this system of getting the main models and using them together in a multi-modular way, you’ll screw up time after time after time, too.

没有飞行员不核对清单就起飞：A、B、C、D……也没有哪个需要再拿两墩的桥牌手，会不对照自己的清单、想清楚打法就去打一手牌。但这些心理学教授自认太聪明，不需要清单。可他们没那么聪明。几乎没人那么聪明。或许根本没人。如果他们用了清单，就会意识到米尔格拉姆实验至少调动了六条心理学原理——而不是三条。他们只需顺着清单走一遍，就能看见自己漏掉了哪些。

“没有飞行员不核对清单就起飞。”

同样地，如果没有这套掌握主要模型、并以多模块方式协同运用它们的体系，你们也会一次又一次地搞砸。

“No pilot takes off without going through his checklist.”没有哪个飞行员不起飞前先过一遍检查清单。

One reason psychology professors so screw up denial is that it’s hard to do demonstrative experiments without conduct forbidden by ethics. To demonstrate how misery creates mental dysfunction in people, think of what you’d have to do to your fellow human beings. And you’d have to do it without telling them about the injury to come. So clearly there are ethical reasons why it’s practically impossible to do the experiments necessary to best lay out the ways human misery creates human mental misfunction.

心理学教授在否认这个问题上之所以如此搞砸，一个原因是：要做演示性实验，难免涉及伦理禁止的行为。要证明苦难如何在人身上造成心理失能，想想你们得对自己的同类做些什么。而且你们还得瞒着他们，不告诉他们即将到来的伤害。所以，很显然，由于伦理上的原因，几乎不可能去做那些必要的实验，来最清楚地展示人类苦难如何造成人类心理失能。

Most professors solve this problem, in effect, by assuming “If I can’t demonstrate it with my experiments, then it doesn’t exist.” However, obviously, that’s asinine. If something is very important but can’t be perfectly and precisely demonstrated because of ethical constraints, you can’t just treat it like it doesn’t exist. You have to do the best you can with it, with such evidence as is available.

大多数教授实际上是通过假定“如果我用实验证明不了它，那它就不存在”来解决这个问题的。然而，这显然荒谬。如果某件事非常重要，却因伦理约束而无法完美、精确地证明，你们也不能就当它不存在。你们必须尽己所能，利用手头可得的证据去处理它。

Pavlov172Ivan PavlovIvan Pavlov (1849–1936) was born in central Russia and attended seminary until age 21, when he abandoned theology in favor of chemistry and physiology. Earning his MD in 1883, he excelled in physiology and surgical techniques. Later, he studied the secretory activity of digestion and ultimately formulated the laws of conditioned reflexes. Pavlov’s most famous experiment showed that dogs tend to salivate before food is actually delivered to their mouths. This result led him to a long series of experiments in which he manipulated the stimuli occurring before the presentation of food. He thereby established the basic laws for the establishment and extinction of what he called “conditional reflexes,” later mistranslated from the original Russian as “conditioned reflexes.” He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1904 for his work on digestive secretions.伊万·巴甫洛夫（Ivan Pavlov，1849–1936 年）生于俄罗斯中部，在神学院读到 21 岁，随后弃神学而选化学和生理学。1883 年他获得医学博士学位，在生理学和外科手术技艺上表现出色。后来，他研究消化液的分泌活动，最终归纳出条件反射的规律。巴甫洛夫最著名的实验表明，狗在食物真正送到嘴边之前就会开始分泌唾液。这一结果引导他进行了一长串实验，在实验中他操控食物呈现之前发生的刺激，从而为他所谓的“条件反射”（conditional reflexes，该词后来由俄语原意误译为 conditioned reflexes）的建立与消退确立了基本规律。1904 年，他因消化液研究获诺贝尔奖。 himself spent the last 10 years of his life torturing dogs. And he published. Thus, we have a vast amount of data about misery-caused mental misfunction in dogs and its correction. Yet it’s in no introductory psychology book that you’ll ever see. SkinnerBorn Burrhus Frederic Skinner in Pennsylvania to an attorney father and a strong and intelligent mother, B. F. Skinner (1904–1990) enjoyed school and did well enough to get to college. Tiring of a bohemian lifestyle, he decided to return to Harvard, where he earned a PhD in psychology. Skinner’s great contributions to psychology are his experiments in operant conditioning and behaviorism. Operant conditioning can be summarized as follows: “A behavior is followed by a consequence, and the nature of the consequence modifies the organism’s tendency to repeat the behavior in the future.”伯尔赫斯·弗雷德里克·斯金纳（B. F. Skinner，1904–1990 年）生于宾夕法尼亚，父亲是律师，母亲坚强而聪慧。他喜欢上学，成绩好到足以升入大学。毕业后，他撰写关于劳工问题的报刊文章，并住在格林威治村。厌倦了波希米亚式的生活后，他决定回到哈佛，在那里获得心理学博士学位。斯金纳对心理学的巨大贡献，是他在操作性条件反射和行为主义方面的实验。操作性条件反射可概括如下：“一个行为之后跟着一个后果，而这个后果的性质会改变该有机体日后重复这一行为的倾向。” by overclaiming when he lapsed into his literary mode, made the drawing of implications from animal behavior into human behavior unpopular. However, for some crazy reason or other, the psychology books are grossly inadequate in dealing with misery-caused mental misfunction.

Pavlov’s most famous experiment showed that dogs tend to salivate before food is actually delivered to their mouths. This result led him to a long series of experiments in which he manipulated the stimuli occurring before the presentation of food. He thereby established the basic laws for the establishment and extinction of what he called “conditional reflexes,” later mistranslated from the original Russian as “conditioned reflexes.” He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1904 for his work on digestive secretions.伊万·巴甫洛夫（Ivan Pavlov，1849–1936 年）生于俄罗斯中部，在神学院读到 21 岁，随后弃神学而选化学和生理学。1883 年他获得医学博士学位，在生理学和外科手术技艺上表现出色。后来，他研究消化液的分泌活动，最终归纳出条件反射的规律。巴甫洛夫最著名的实验表明，狗在食物真正送到嘴边之前就会开始分泌唾液。这一结果引导他进行了一长串实验，在实验中他操控食物呈现之前发生的刺激，从而为他所谓的“条件反射”（conditional reflexes，该词后来由俄语原意误译为 conditioned reflexes）的建立与消退确立了基本规律。1904 年，他因消化液研究获诺贝尔奖。（Pavlov）本人在生命的最后十年里一直在折磨狗。而且他发表了成果。因此，我们拥有大量关于狗因苦难而致心理失能及其矫正的数据。然而，你们在任何一本心理学入门书里都看不到这些。我不知道是因为他们不喜欢巴甫洛夫折磨狗这件事，还是因为 B. F. 斯金纳197B. F. SkinnerB·F·斯金纳（B. F. Skinner）在陷入文学腔调时言过其实，使得从动物行为推及人类行为这件事变得不受欢迎。但不管出于什么荒唐原因，心理学书籍在处理“苦难导致的心理失能”时都严重欠缺。

You may say, “What difference does all this psychological ignorance make?” Well, if I’m right, you need these models that are blanked out by this ignorance. And, furthermore, you need them in a form whereby if there are 20 constructs, you have all 20. In other words, you shouldn’t be operating with 10. And you need to use them as a checklist. So you have to go back and put in your own head what I’d call the psychology of misjudgment in a form whereby you have all of the important models and you can use them. And you especially need them when four or five forces from these models come together to operate in the same direction. In such cases, you often get lollapalooza effects—which can make you rich, or they can kill you. So it’s essential that you beware of lollapalooza effects.

你们也许会说：“这种心理学上的无知，又有什么关系？”嗯，如果我说得对，你们就需要这些被无知遮蔽了的模型。而且，你们需要的是这样一套形式：如果有20个构件，你们就得掌握全部20个。换句话说，你们不该只掌握10个。你们需要把它们当作核查清单来用。所以你们必须回过头去，把我认为应称为“误判心理学”的东西装进自己的头脑，其形式要能让你们掌握所有重要模型并运用它们。尤其当四五种力量从这些模型中汇聚、朝同一方向作用时，你们格外需要它们。在这种情况下，你们常常会遭遇 lollapalooza 效应——它能让你致富，也能要你的命。所以，警惕 lollapalooza 效应是必不可少的。

There’s only one right way to do it: You have to get the main doctrines together and use them as a checklist. And, to repeat for emphasis, you have to pay special attention to combinatorial effects that create lollapalooza consequences.

做这件事只有一条正确的路：你们必须把主要原理汇集起来，当作核查清单来用。而且，为了强调，我要重复一遍：你们必须特别留意那些造成 lollapalooza 后果的组合效应。

“You have to get the main doctrines together and use them as a checklist. And you have to pay special attention to combinatorial effects that create lollapalooza consequences.”你必须把主要原理汇集起来，当作一张检查清单来用。你还要特别关注那些会引发『合力效应』（lollapalooza）的组合作用。

You can also learn when you’re playing the game of persuasion—for a reputable reason—to combine these forces in a way that makes you more effective. Let me give you an example of that—of wise psychology of yore. In Captain [James] Cook’s174Captain James Cook day, he took these long voyages. At the time, scurvy was the dread of the long voyage. In scurvy, your living gums putrefy in your mouth, after which the disease gets unpleasant and kills you. And being on a primitive sailing ship with a bunch of dying sailors is a very awkward business.

当你们出于正当理由玩说服这门游戏时，也可以学会把这些力量组合起来，让自己更有成效。

So everybody was terribly interested in scurvy, but they didn’t know about vitamin C. Well, Captain Cook, being a smart man with a multiple-models kind of approach, noticed that Dutch ships had less scurvy than English ships on long voyages. So he said, “What are the Dutch doing that’s different?” And he noticed they had all these barrels of sauerkraut. So he thought, “I’m going on these long voyages, and it’s very dangerous. Sauerkraut may help.” So he laid in all this sauerkraut, which, incidentally, happens to contain a trace of vitamin C.

所以人人都对坏血病极为关切，但他们并不知道维生素C。嗯，库克船长是个聪明人，用的是多模型那一套思路，他注意到荷兰（Dutch）船在长期航行中坏血病比英国（English）船少。于是他说：“荷兰人做了什么不一样的事？”他注意到他们有那么多桶酸菜。所以他想：“我要进行这些长途航行，非常危险。酸菜或许有用。”于是他贮备了大量酸菜——顺便说一句，酸菜恰好含有微量的维生素C。

But English sailors were a tough, cranky, and dangerous bunch in that day. They hated “krauts.” And they were used to their standard food and booze. So how do you get such English sailors to eat sauerkraut?

但那时的英国水手是一帮粗野、暴躁又危险的人。他们讨厌“krauts（德国佬的酸菜）”。而且他们习惯了标准配给的食物和酒。那么，你怎么让这样的英国水手吃酸菜呢？

Well, Cook didn’t want to tell ’em that he was doing it in the hope it would prevent scurvy—because they might mutiny and take over the ship if they thought that he was taking them on a voyage so long that scurvy was likely. So here’s what he did: Officers ate at one place where the men could observe them. And for a long time, he served sauerkraut to the officers but not to the men. And then, finally, Captain Cook said, “Well, the men can have it one day a week.” In due course, he had the whole crew eating sauerkraut.

嗯，库克不想告诉他们，他这么做是希望预防坏血病——因为如果水手们以为他带他们进行的是一段漫长到很可能染上坏血病的航程，可能会哗变夺船。于是他是这么做的：军官在一个水手能观察到的地方用餐。很长一段时间里，他只给军官上酸菜，不给普通水手上。最后，库克船长说：“好吧，水手们每周可以有一天吃上它。”久而久之，他让全体船员都吃上了酸菜。

I regard that as a very constructive use of elementary psychology. It may have saved God knows how many lives and caused God knows how much achievement. However, if you don’t know the right techniques, you can’t use them.

我认为这是对基础心理学一次极具建设性的运用。它或许挽救了天知道多少条性命，成就了天知道多少功业。然而，如果你们不懂正确的技巧，就用不上它们。

Worldly wisdom is mostly very, very simple. And what I’m urging on you is not that hard to do if you have the will to plow through and do it. And the rewards are awesome—absolutely awesome. But maybe you aren’t interested in awesome rewards or avoiding a lot of misery or being more able to serve everything you love in life. And if that’s your attitude, then don’t pay attention to what I’ve been trying to tell you, because you’re already on the right track.

世俗智慧大体上非常、非常简单。而只要你们有毅力去啃下并践行，我敦促你们做的这件事并不难。回报是惊人的——绝对惊人。但也许你们对惊人的回报没兴趣，对避免大量苦难没兴趣，对更有能力去服务生命中珍爱的一切没兴趣。如果你们是这种态度，那就不必理会我一直在讲的这些，因为你们已经走在正确的路上了。

It can’t be emphasized too much that issues of morality are deeply entwined with worldly wisdom considerations involving psychology. For example, take the issue of stealing. A very significant fraction of the people in the world will steal if a) it’s very easy to do and b) there’s practically no chance of being caught. And once they start stealing, the consistency principle—which is a big part of human psychology—will soon combine with operant conditioning to make stealing habitual. So if you run a business where it’s easy to steal because of your methods, you’re working a great moral injury on the people who work for you.

道德问题深深地与涉及心理学的世俗智慧考量交织在一起，这一点怎么强调都不为过。举个例子，说说偷窃问题。世界上很大一部分人，只要 a) 极易下手、且 b) 几乎不可能被抓，就会去偷。而一旦他们开始偷，一致性原理——人类心理学的一大组成部分——很快就会与操作性条件反射结合起来，让偷窃变成习惯。所以，如果你们经营的企业，因其方法之故让偷窃易如反掌，那你们就是在对自己手下的人造成巨大的道德伤害。

“道德问题深深地与涉及心理学的世俗智慧考量交织在一起。”

“Issues of morality are deeply entwined with worldly wisdom considerations involvingxa0psychology.”道德议题，与关乎心理学的世俗智慧考量深深纠缠在一起。

Again, that’s obvious. It’s very, very important to create human systems that are hard to cheat. Otherwise, you’re ruining your civilization, because these big incentives will create incentive-caused bias and people will rationalize that bad behavior is okay. Then, if somebody else does it, now you’ve got at least two psychological principles: incentive-caused bias plus social proof. Not only that but you get Serpico176SerpicoSerpico (1973) was a popular film directed by Sidney Lumet, based on the book by journalist Peter Maas. The plot concerns undercover police officer Frank Serpico, who does his best arresting criminals of all types, but especially drug dealers, despite working in a corrupt police department. Serpico refuses to accept bribes and becomes sufficiently appalled at his shady colleagues that he testifies against them, thus placing his life in jeopardy. Al Pacino appeared in the title role and earned an Academy Award nomination for his acting. The film was also nominated for a screenwriting Oscar.《冲突》（Serpico，1973 年）是西德尼·吕美特（Sidney Lumet）执导的一部热门影片，改编自记者彼得·马斯（Peter Maas）的著作。剧情围绕卧底警察弗兰克·塞尔皮科（Frank Serpico）展开，他在一个腐败的警察局里尽职缉捕各类罪犯，尤其是毒贩。塞尔皮科拒绝受贿，对那群手脚不干净的同事厌恶到了出庭指证他们的程度，从而把自己的生命置于险境。阿尔·帕西诺（Al Pacino）主演该片并获奥斯卡表演奖提名。该片还获得了编剧奖提名。 effects: If enough people are profiting in a general social climate of doing wrong, then they’ll turn on you and become dangerous enemies if you try and blow the whistle. It’s very dangerous to ignore these principles and let slop creep in. Powerful psychological forces are at work for evil.

再者，这是显而易见的事。创建难以作弊181Cheating作弊的人类体系，非常、非常重要。否则，你们就是在毁掉自己的文明，因为这些巨大的激励会产生“激励导致的偏见”，而人们会为不良行为找到“这没什么大不了”的借口。然后，如果别人也这么做，你们现在就至少有了两条心理学原理：激励导致的偏见，加上社会认同。不仅如此，你们还会遭遇“瑟皮科效应”：如果在普遍作恶的社会氛围中，有足够多的人正在从中牟利，那么当你们试图揭发时，他们就会倒戈，变成危险的敌人。

忽视这些原理、任由污烂（slop）渗入，是非常危险的。强大的心理力量正在为恶运作。

How does this relate to the law business? Well, people graduate from places like Stanford Law School and go into the legislatures of our nation and, with the best of motives, pass laws that are easily used by people to cheat. Well, there could hardly be a worse thing you could do.

这和律师行业有什么关系？嗯，人们从斯坦福法学院这类地方毕业，进入我们国家的立法机构，怀着最良好的动机，却通过了极易被人用来作弊的法律。嗯，这大概是你所能做的最糟糕的事了。

Let’s say you have a desire to do public service. As a natural part of your planning, you think in reverse and ask, “What can I do to ruin our civilization?” That’s easy. If what you want to do is to ruin your civilization, just go to the legislature and pass laws that create systems wherein people can easily cheat. It will work perfectly.181Cheating作弊

假设你们有从事公共服务的愿望。作为规划的天然一环，你们不妨反过来想，问一句：“我要怎么做才能毁掉我们的文明？”这很容易。如果你们想毁掉自己的文明，只需走进立法机构，通过一些法律，造出人们可以轻易作弊的体系。它会完美奏效。

Take the workers’ compensation system in California. Stress is real. And its misery can be real. So you want to compensate people for their stress in the workplace. It seems like a noble thing to do. But the trouble with such a compensation practice is that it’s practically impossible to delete huge cheating. And once you reward cheating, you get crooked lawyers, crooked doctors, crooked unions, etc. participating in referral schemes. You get a total miasma of disastrous behavior. And the behavior makes all the people doing it worse as they do it. So you were trying to help your civilization, but what you did was create enormous damage, net. So it’s much better to let some things go uncompensated—to let life be hard—than to create systems that are easy to cheat.

以加利福尼亚（California）的工人赔偿制度为例。压力是真实的，其造成的苦难也可以是真实的。所以你们想补偿人们职场中的压力。这看来是件高尚的事。但这种补偿做法的麻烦在于，几乎不可能杜绝大规模的作弊。而一旦你们奖励了作弊，就会引来看歪门邪道的律师、医生、工会等等参与转介勾当。你们得到的是一片灾难性行为的瘴气。而且这种行为会让所有参与者越陷越坏。所以，你们本想帮助文明，结果净效果却是造成了巨大损害。因此，与其创造出易于作弊的体系，不如让某些事情得不到补偿——让生活保持艰难。

Let me give you an example: I have a friend who made an industrial product at a plant in Texas not far from the border. He was in a low-margin, tough business. He got massive fraud in the workers’ compensation system, to the point that his premiums reached double-digit percentages of payroll. And it was not that dangerous to produce his product. It’s not like he was a demolition contractor or something.

我给你们举个例子：我有个朋友，在离边境不远的得克萨斯（Texas）一家工厂生产工业品。他干的是低利润、高难度的买卖。他在工人赔偿制度中遭遇了大规模欺诈，以至于他的保费达到了工资总额的两位数百分比。而生产他的产品其实并不那么危险，他又不是拆毁承包商之类。

So he pleaded with the union, “You’ve got to stop this. There’s not enough money in making this product to cover all of this fraud.” But by then, everyone’s used to it. “It’s extra income. It’s extra money. Everybody does it. It can’t be that wrong. Eminent lawyers, eminent doctors, eminent chiropractors—if there are any such things—are cheating.”

于是他恳求工会：“你们必须制止这件事。生产这种产品赚的钱，根本不够填补所有这些欺诈。”但到那时，人人都已习以为常。“这是额外收入。这是外快。大家都在干。不至于那么错。顶尖的律师、顶尖的医生、顶尖的脊椎按摩师——如果真有这种人的话——都在作弊。”

And no one could tell them, “You can’t do it anymore.” Incidentally, that’s Pavlovian mere association, too. When people get bad news, they hate the messenger. Therefore, it was very hard for the union representative to tell all of these people that the easy money was about to stop. That is not the way to advance as a union representative.

而没人能告诉他们：“你们不能再这么干了。”顺便说一句，这也是巴甫洛夫式的单纯联想。当人们得到坏消息时，他们憎恨传消息的人。因此，工会代表很难去告诉所有这些人大笔的容易钱就要停了。那可不是当工会代表往上爬的办法。

So my friend closed his plant and moved the work to Utah among a community of believing Mormons. Well, the Mormons aren’t into workers’ compensation fraud—at least they aren’t in my friend’s plant. And guess what his workers’ compensation expense is today? It’s 2 percent of payroll.

于是我的朋友关掉了工厂，把活儿搬到了犹他（Utah），在一群虔诚的摩门（Mormon）教徒社区中生产。嗯，摩门教徒不搞工人赔偿欺诈——至少在我朋友的工厂里不这么干。猜猜他今天的工人赔偿开支是多少？工资总额的2%。

This sort of tragedy is caused by letting the slop run. You must stop slop early. It’s very hard to stop slop and moral failure if you let it run for a while.

这类悲剧，源于任由污烂蔓延。你们必须及早制止污烂。如果放任它跑一阵子，就极难再刹住污烂与道德败坏。

“你们必须及早制止污烂。如果放任它跑一阵子，就极难再刹住污烂与道德败坏。”

“You must stop slop early. It’s very hard to stop slop and moral failure if you let it run for axa0while.”你必须在苗头初现时便刹住敷衍。一旦任其蔓延，便很难再阻止敷衍与道德溃败。

Of course, as I said before, there is one big consideration that needs huge and special attention as part of any use of techniques deliberately harnessing elementary psychological forces, and that is that once you know how to do it, there are real moral limits regarding how much you should do it. Not all of what you know how to do should you use to manipulate people.

当然，正如我之前所说，只要是有意驾驭基础心理力量，其技术应用就有一项需要极度特别留意的重大考量，那就是：一旦你们懂得了怎么做，就存在一个真实的道德限度，限定你们应当做到什么程度。并非所有你们懂得怎么做的事，都该用来操控他人。

Also, if you’re willing to transcend the moral limits and the person you’re trying to manipulate realizes what you’re doing because he also understands the psychology, he’ll hate you. There is wonderfully persuasive evidence of this effect taken from labor relations, some in Israel. So not only are there moral objections, but there are also practical objections—big ones in some cases.

此外，如果你们甘愿跨越道德限度，而被你们试图操控的人因为也懂心理学、看穿了你们的所作所为，他就会恨你们。关于这种效应，有极具说服力的证据取自劳资关系，其中有些发生在以色列。所以不仅有道德上的反对，也有实际上的反对——在某些情况下还是极大的反对。

Audience question: How do you incorporate psychology in your investment decisions? I think it would be more than just picking products that will appeal to everybody, like Coke. After all, there are a lot of smart people out there who obviously think just the way you showed us today. So are you looking for failure in the thinking of other investors when you go about picking successful companies?

听众提问：您是如何把心理学融入投资决策的？我想这应该不只是挑选那些会受大众欢迎的产品，比如可口可乐192Coca-cola可口可乐。毕竟，外面有很多聪明人，他们的思维方式显然就和您今天展示给我们的一样。那么，您在挑选成功的公司时，是在寻找其他投资者思维中的漏洞吗？

What makes investment hard, as I said at USC, is that it’s easy to see that some companies have better businesses than others. But the price of the stock goes up so high that all of a sudden, the question of which stock is the best to buy gets quite difficult. We’ve never eliminated the difficulty of that problem. And 98 percent of the time, our attitude toward the market is that we’re agnostics. We don’t know. Is GM valued properly vis-xe0-vis Ford? We don’t know.

正如我在南加大所说，投资之所以难，在于很容易看出有些公司比其他公司拥有更好的生意。但股价会涨得那么高，以至于突然之间，“哪只股票最值得买”这个问题变得相当困难。我们从未消除这个问题的难度。98%的时候，我们对待市场的态度是不可知论者。我们不知道。通用汽车（GM）相对福特（Ford）的估值合理吗？我们不知道。

We’re always looking for something where we think we have an insight that gives us a big statistical advantage. Sometimes it comes from psychology, but often it comes from something else. And we only find a few, maybe one or two a year. We have no system for having automatic good judgment on all investment decisions that can be made. Ours is a totally different system. We just look for no-brainer decisions. As Buffett and I say over and over again, we don’t leap 7-foot fences. Instead, we look for 1-foot fences with big rewards on the other side. So we’ve succeeded by making the world easy for ourselves, not by solving hard problems.

我们总是在寻找那样的东西：我们认为自己拥有某种洞见，能带来巨大的统计优势。有时这洞见来自心理学，但常常来自别的方面。我们一年只找到寥寥几个，或许一两个。我们没有任何一套系统，能对一切可做的投资决策自动给出良好判断。我们的系统完全不同。我们只是寻找那些“不假思索”的决定。正如巴菲特和我反复说的，我们不去跨越七英尺高的栅栏，而是寻找那另一边有大把回报的一英尺高的栅栏。所以我们成功，靠的是让世界对我们来说变得容易，而不是靠解决难题。

7-foot fences
“We just look for no-brainer decisions. As Buffett and I say over and over again, we don’t leap 7-foot fences. Instead, we look for 1-foot fences with big rewards on the otherxa0side.”我们只寻找不假思索就能做的决定。正如巴菲特和我反复说的：我们不跳七英尺高的栏。我们找的是另一侧摆着丰厚回报的一英尺矮栏。

Based on statistical analysis and insight?

基于统计分析和洞察力吗？

Well, certainly when we do make a decision, we think that we have an insight advantage. And it’s true that some of the insight is statistical in nature. However, again, we find only a few of those. It doesn’t help us merely for favorable odds to exist. They have to be in a place where we can recognize them. So it takes a mispriced opportunity that we’re smart enough to recognize. And that combination doesn’t occur often. But it doesn’t have to. If you wait for the big opportunity and have the courage and vigor to grasp it firmly when it arrives, how many do you need? For example, take the top 10 business investments Berkshire Hathaway’s ever made. We would be very rich if we’d never done anything else—in two lifetimes.

嗯，当然，当我们确实做出决定时，我们认为自己拥有洞见上的优势。而且的确，某些洞见本质上具有统计性。然而，再一次地，我们只找到寥寥几个。仅仅存在有利的赔率，对我们并无帮助。它们必须出现在我们能够识别的地方。所以需要的是一个被错误定价的机会，且我们足够聪明去识别它。而这种组合并不常出现。但没必要常出现。如果你们等待重大机会，并在它到来时鼓起勇气和干劲牢牢抓住，你们需要多少个？举个例子，看看伯克希尔·哈撒韦有史以来最成功的十笔商业投资。即便我们两辈子别的什么都不做，只做这十笔，也早已非常富有了。

So, once again, we don’t have any system for giving you perfect investment judgment on all subjects at all times. That would be ridiculous. I’m just trying to give you a method you can use to sift reality to obtain an occasional opportunity for rational reaction. If you take that method into something as competitive as common stock picking, you’re competing with many brilliant people. So even with our method, we only get a few opportunities. Fortunately, that happens to be enough.

所以，我要再次说明，我们没有任何一套系统，能随时对所有主题给出完美的投资判断。那才荒谬。我只是想给你们一种方法，让你们可以筛滤现实，偶尔获得理性反应的机会。如果你们把这种方法用到像选普通股这样竞争激烈的领域，你们是在和许多聪明人竞争。所以即便用我们的方法，我们也只得到寥寥几个机会。所幸，这恰好够了。

Have you been successful in creating an atmosphere where people below you can do the same things you’re talking about doing yourself? For example, you talked about the tendency toward commitment and consistency…

您是否成功地营造出这样一种氛围，让您下属的人也能做到您所说的那些您自己正在做的事？比如，您谈到了承诺与一致性倾向……

Mostly about the terrible mistakes it causes you to make.

主要关于它导致你们犯下的可怕错误。

How have you created an atmosphere comfortable enough for people to abandon that tendency and admit that they’ve made a mistake? For example, someone here earlier this year from Intel talked about problems that occurred with their Pentium chip.179Pentium Chip奔腾芯片 One of the most difficult things for them to do was to realize they’d been going about it the wrong way and turn course. And it’s very difficult to do that in a complex structure. How do you foster that?

您是如何营造出足够宽松的氛围，让人们得以放下那种倾向、承认自己犯了错？比如，今年早些时候，来自英特尔（Intel）的一位听众谈到他们奔腾（Pentium）芯片出现的问题。对他们来说最难的事情之一，就是意识到自己一直以来的做法是错的，然后改弦更张。而在一个复杂的结构里，做到这一点非常困难。您是如何培养这种氛围的？

Intel and its ilk create a coherent culture where teams solve difficult problems on the cutting edge of science. That’s radically different from Berkshire Hathaway. Berkshire is a holding company. We’ve decentralized all the power, except for natural headquarters-type capital allocation.

英特尔（Intel）及其同类企业，营造出一种步调一致的文化，让团队去攻克科学前沿的难题。这与伯克希尔·哈撒韦截然不同。伯克希尔是一家控股公司。除了天然属于总部性质的资本配置之外，我们把所有权力都下放了。

By and large, we’ve chosen people we admire enormously to have the power beneath us. It’s easy for us to get along with them, on average, because we love and admire them. And they create the culture for whatever invention and reality recognition is going on in their businesses. And included in that reality recognition is the recognition that previous conclusions were incorrect.

大体上，我们挑选的是我们极为钦佩的人，把权力交到他们手中。平均而言，我们和他们相处融洽，因为我们爱戴并钦佩他们。而他们为自己企业中的发明创造和现实认知营造了文化。这种现实认知之中，也包含了对“先前结论有误”的认知。

But we’re a totally different kind of company. It’s not at all clear to me that Warren or I would be that good at doing what Andy Grove180Andy GroveBorn Andr\xe1s Gr\xf3f in Budapest, Hungary, Andy Grove (1936–2016) earned a bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering from the City College of New York and a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He worked at Fairchild Semiconductor before becoming the fourth employee at the nascent Intel Corporation. He became Intel’s president in 1979, its CEO in 1987, and its chairman and CEO in 1997. Author of several academic and mass trade books, his 1996 work Only the Paranoid Survive was hugely popular. It’s on Charlie’s recommended book list.安迪·格鲁夫（Andy Grove，1936–2016 年）生于匈牙利布达佩斯，原名 András Gróf，从纽约城市学院获得化学工程学士学位，又从加州大学伯克利分校获得博士学位。他曾在仙童半导体（Fairchild Semiconductor）工作，之后成为初创的英特尔（Intel）公司的第四名员工。他 1979 年出任英特尔总裁，1987 年任 CEO，1997 年任董事长兼 CEO。他著有多部学术和大众畅销书，1996 年的《只有偏执狂才能生存》（Only the Paranoid Survive）大受欢迎，也在查理的推荐书单上。 does. We don’t have special competence in that field. We are fairly good at relating to brilliant people we love. But we have defects. For example, some regard me as absentminded and opinionated. I might be a mess at Intel. However, both Warren and I are very good at changing our prior conclusions. We work at developing that facility because without it, disaster often comes.

但我们是一家完全不同的公司。我一点都不确定，沃伦或我能不能把安迪·格鲁夫180Andy GroveBorn Andr\xe1s Gr\xf3f in Budapest, Hungary, Andy Grove (1936–2016) earned a bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering from the City College of New York and a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. He worked at Fairchild Semiconductor before becoming the fourth employee at the nascent Intel Corporation. He became Intel’s president in 1979, its CEO in 1987, and its chairman and CEO in 1997. Author of several academic and mass trade books, his 1996 work Only the Paranoid Survive was hugely popular. It’s on Charlie’s recommended book list.安迪·格鲁夫（Andy Grove，1936–2016 年）生于匈牙利布达佩斯，原名 András Gróf，从纽约城市学院获得化学工程学士学位，又从加州大学伯克利分校获得博士学位。他曾在仙童半导体（Fairchild Semiconductor）工作，之后成为初创的英特尔（Intel）公司的第四名员工。他 1979 年出任英特尔总裁，1987 年任 CEO，1997 年任董事长兼 CEO。他著有多部学术和大众畅销书，1996 年的《只有偏执狂才能生存》（Only the Paranoid Survive）大受欢迎，也在查理的推荐书单上。（Andy Grove）所做的事做得那么好。我们在那个领域没有特殊才能。我们相当擅长与我们所爱的聪明人相处。但我们也有缺点。比如，有人觉得我心不在焉又固执己见。在英特尔我可能会一团糟。不过，沃伦和我都非常擅长改变自己先前的结论。我们努力培养这种能力，因为没有它，灾难往往就会降临。

Would you talk a little bit about your seeming predilection away from investing in high-technology stocks, on your own part and the part of Berkshire Hathaway? One of the things I’ve found eye-opening and a little surprising is how the difficulties of running a low-tech business and those of running a high-tech business aren’t all that different.

能否请您谈谈，无论对您个人还是对伯克希尔·哈撒韦而言，您那种明显不愿投资高科技股票的偏好？有一件事让我大开眼界、也略感意外：经营一家低科技生意和经营一家高科技生意，其困难之处其实并没有那么不同。

They’re all hard. But why should it be easy to get rich? In a competitive world, shouldn’t it be impossible for there to be an easy way for everybody to get rich? Of course they’re all hard.

它们都很难。但致富凭什么该是容易的？在一个竞争的世界里，难道不该是：不可能存在一种让人人都能轻松致富的捷径吗？它们当然都很难。

The reason we’re not in high-tech businesses is that we have a special lack of aptitude in that area. And yes—a low-tech business can be plenty hard. Just try to open a restaurant and make it succeed.

我们不涉足高科技生意的原因，是我们在那个领域特别地缺乏天分。而且没错——低科技生意也可以相当难。试试开一家餐馆并让它成功就知道了。

“低科技生意也可以相当难。试试开一家餐馆并让它成功就知道了。”

“A low-tech business can be plenty hard. Just try to open a restaurant and make itxa0succeed.”低技术生意也可能相当难做。你只管去开家餐馆，并把它做成功试试。

You seem to be suggesting that there’s special aptitude required in high-tech businesses—that they’re harder. But aren’t they equally difficult?

您似乎在高科技生意需要特殊天赋——它们更难——这一点上有所暗示。可它们不是同样难吗？

The advantage of low-tech stuff for us is that we think we understand it fairly well. The other stuff we don’t. And we’d rather deal with what we understand. Why should we want to play a competitive game in a field where we have no advantage—maybe a disadvantage—instead of in a field where we have a clear advantage?

低科技的东西对我们的优势在于，我们认为自己相当理解它。别的东西我们不懂。而我们宁愿处理自己理解的东西。我们何必在一个毫无优势——甚至可能是劣势——的领域去玩竞争游戏，而不在一个我们有明显优势的领域玩呢？

Each of you will have to figure out where your talents lie. And you’ll have to use your advantages. But if you try to succeed in what you’re worst at, you’re going to have a very lousy career. I can almost guarantee it. To do otherwise, you’d have to buy a winning lottery ticket or get very lucky somewhere else.

你们每个人都得弄清楚自己的才能在哪里，并且善用自己的优势。但如果你们试图在自己最不擅长的领域取得成功，你们的职业生涯会很糟糕。这一点我几乎可以保证。要想不这样，你们就得买中一张中奖彩票，或在别的什么地方极为走运。

Warren Buffett has said that the investment Berkshire made in an airline was a good example of what not to do. What chain of thinking led to that wrong decision?

沃伦·巴菲特曾说，伯克希尔在航空公司上的投资是“不该做什么”的典型例子。是怎样的思维链条导致了那个错误决定？

We were not buying stock in USAir on the theory that the common shareholders were certain to prosper, because the history of the airline business in terms of taking care of shareholders has been terrible. It was a preferred stock with a mandatory redemption. In effect, we were loaning money to USAir, and we had this equity kicker. We weren’t guessing whether it would be a great place for the shareholders. We were guessing whether it would remain prosperous enough to pay off a credit instrument, carrying a fixed dividend and a mandatory redemption. And we guessed that the business would not get so bad that we’d have a credit threat for which we were not being adequately compensated by the high rate we were getting.

我们买入全美航空（USAir）股票，并非基于“普通股股东必定兴旺”的理论，因为航空业在善待股东方面的历史一直很糟。我们买的是带有强制赎回条款的优先股。实际上，我们是借钱给全美航空，并附带这个股权甜头。我们并没有去猜它会不会是股东的好去处。我们猜的是，它能否保持足够的兴旺，以偿付那张带有固定股息和强制赎回的信用工具。而我们猜的是：这门生意不至于糟到让我们面临信用风险，且我们得到的高利率并未对此给予充分补偿。

As it happened, USAir went right to the brink of going broke. It was hanging by a thread for several months. It’s since come back. And we’ll probably get all our money back plus the whole coupon. But it was a mistake. [Editor’s note: Berkshire did indeed come out whole on its USAir investment.]

结果，全美航空一度走到破产边缘。有好几个月它都命悬一线。后来它缓了过来。我们大概能拿回全部本金外加全部票息。但那是个错误。［编者按：伯克希尔在全美航空的投资上确实全身而退。］

I don’t want you to think we have any way of learning or behaving so you won’t make a lot of mistakes. I’m just saying that you can learn to make fewer mistakes than other people—and how to fix your mistakes faster when you do make them. But there’s no way that you can live an adequate life without making many mistakes. Part of what you must learn is how to handle mistakes and new facts that change the odds. Life, in part, is like a poker game, wherein you have to learn to quit sometimes when holding a much-loved hand.

我不想让你们以为，我们有什么办法能学会或表现得让你们不犯许多错误。我只是说，你们可以学着比别人犯更少的错——并且在真的犯错时，更快地修正。但你们不可能不犯许多错误而度过堪称合格的一生。你们必须学会的一部分，是如何处理错误，以及处理那些改变赔率的新事实。人生在某种程度上就像一局扑克牌，你们得学会：有时手里握着极珍爱的牌，也得学会弃局。

“你们不可能不犯许多错误而度过堪称合格的一生。你们必须学会的一部分，是如何处理错误，以及处理那些改变赔率的新事实。”
